items.content: Prather: One of the things that our survey reveals is what happens in between these elections. What you can see is a decline over time. So, much of the loss in trust among Republicans happened in the intervening years, not as a result of the election itself. So if you just looked at where Republican trust was post-2024 and then looked at it post-2026, you'd see this huge, massive decline. Most of that decline happened across January and then January to September, and really we only see a 6-percentage-point decline in trust from September to November. So that suggests to us there's something going on that's different.

items.title: DC votes for the Royals Hall of Fame, Part 1
items.author: SRS0=+its=JF=mg-d0.substack.com=bounce+9ddca1.63af5d-misc=muneer.top@eforward.registrar-servers.com
items.content:
Now that the dust has settled from the 2026 mid-terms, we can turn our attention to another election chock full of debate and controversy…the election for the Royals Hall of Fame Class of 2027.

This is the first time we are seeing some of the names from the ‘14 and ‘15 teams on the ballot, it will be fascinating to see who gets the nod and who doesn’t.

Royals Hall of Fame Voting (Regular Phase) - 2027 Rules and Guidelines for Eligibility

Royals Hall of Fame Voting (Regular Phase) shall be completed annually with electors consisting of the following: (1) All living members of the Royals Hall of Fame (2) Royals Ownership (3) Members of the Royals Hall of Fame Executive Board (4) Royals Associates with 15 years or more service (5) Select members of the Kansas City Chapter of the Baseball Writers of America and Kansas City media members (6) Royals Fans to be represented as twelve electors via on-line balloting (Fan Vote Distribution: twelve full votes for each of the top five vote getters).

To be eligible for the first time Royals Alumni must have been active in the Major Leagues at some time during a period beginning twelve (12) years before and ending three (3) years or more prior to election. Eligible alumni that received a minimum of ten percent (10%) of the vote in the most recent prior election cycle remain on the ballot for up to five cycles. All eligible alumni must have been active with the Kansas City Royals for at least three (3) seasons and accumulated a minimum of 1,500 plate appearances or 300 innings pitched; managers must have led the Royals for at least the equivalent of three full seasons. Those eligible shall have ceased to be an active on-field member of the Kansas City Royals (or for any other Major League Organization) in the role for which they are being considered for at least three (3) calendar years preceding the election – but may be otherwise connected to the Royals or another Major League Organization.

Any eligible alumni receiving votes on seventy-five percent (75%) of the ballots cast will be deemed an elected Royals Hall of Fame member. To remain on the ballot for the next RHOF voting cycle, eligible alumni must receive a minimum of ten percent (10%) of the ballots cast. In even numbered years, at the discretion of the Royals Hall of Fame Executive Board, a separate Veterans Committee vote can consider the candidacy of non-player personnel and alumni who previously received Royals Hall of Fame Voting (Regular Phase) votes but are no longer eligible for election in that manner. —- from www.royals.com

There are 12 players on the ballot, you can vote for up to 5. First let’s look at the two players on the ballot for the final time…

Combine that production with the effortless outfield defense he played during the first half of his career and you have one of the best all around baseball players of this century. The Baseball Writers of America recognized that by voting Beltran into the Baseball Hall of Fame last summer.

  • Batting Average - 3rd (.295)

  • On-base Percentage - 6th (.359)

  • Slugging Percentage - 7th (.449)

There’s absolutely no denying that Billy Butler is in a group with Hal McRae, Mike Sweeney, and now Bobby Witt Jr as the greatest right-handed hitters in club history.

There’s also no sane way to justify not voting Butler into the Royals Hall of Fame. Besides, the guy has the best nickname in team history. Who doesn’t like a big helping of Country Breakfast?

There are four players on the Royals Hall of Fame ballot for the first time this year. Let’s look at each of them, and we’ll cover the other 6 returning names on the ballot next time.

Hosmer was a very good player in Kansas City, albeit with some holes in his game that he never really closed up. Take a look at the 8 offensive categories I listed for Butler above.

In how many of those categories do you think Hosmer ranks above Butler?

Hosmer and Butler are tied with 127 homers as a Royal, otherwise Butler clears Hoz in every category.

Hosmer was also unquestionably the leader of the ‘14 and ‘15 squads, and that’s what tips the scales for me. It might come as a surprise to some, but I’m a YES on Hosmer for the Royals Hall of Fame.

Here’s the important thing….if you vote for Hosmer you absolutely have to vote for Butler as well.

Before we move on, let me share my favorite Hosmer clip….

Moose also authored one of the greatest post-season plays of all time in Game 3 of the 2014 ALCS…

I’m a NO on him for the HOF

Ok, that leaves 6 more players to discuss, all of whom have been on the ballot before. We’ll talk about Lorenzo Cain, Alcides Escobar, Joakim Soria, Greg Holland, Wade Davis, and Kelvin Herrera in the next edition of the Diamond Chronicles!

items.title: New from Chicago: A journey through Rome's history and archaeology as seen in a single city block
items.author: 558757297.1998257.813949133233@e2ma.net
items.content:
Delve into Rome’s lost history through the stories of a single city block.

Cutting through the heart of Rome is Via delle Botteghe Oscure, a time-worn street named for the mysterious “shops” said to run beneath it. History lies thick here, a museum atop a convent atop ancient ruins; layered in are traces of artisans and poets, pilgrims and saints, a Fascist deportation, a communist coffee bar, a political assassination, and shopkeepers, too. These stories all rest upon a single city block, the same place where, in 13 BCE, the triumphal Roman general Lucius Cornelius Balbus built a monumental theater complex in his own honor.

Elizabeth Rodini’s digs deep into this corner of the city, uncovering a set of surprising, often poignant narratives that range across two thousand years. For as the walls of Balbus’s compound decayed and the neighborhood was rebuilt, this block would come to shelter Romans from all walks of life: the daughters of local prostitutes, an earnest young man in search of a bride, an entrepreneur determined to preserve the city’s colorful dialect, a Jewish family recently liberated from the nearby Ghetto, and a band of idealistic archaeologists unearthing a long-forgotten past, as well as a gifted baker, a medieval donkey, and a Renaissance ghost. Their stories survive in archives and artifacts but also in the enduring power of rumor and legend.

On the Street of the Hidden Shops invites us on a captivating journey to one place across many centuries. Its tight urban focus reveals a Rome most visitors miss, while uncovering some of the many Romes that have been largely lost to history.

items.title: Leadership Dispatch: Use positive language
items.author: bounces+38uqqg6p9kfkhr65vo9urh445opwzs7h57lq@ckespa.joshdoody.com
items.content:
This week's Leadership Dispatch is about how to communicate more effectively by using positive language. There are two main reasons you should consider communicating this way: You'll be perceived as more collaborative and easier to work with; when you need to deliver bad news using negative language, you'll get much more attention.

Use positive language whenever possible.

When you set a positive tone for your conversations you will be perceived as more collaborative than combative or resistant, and people will feel better about working with you. And when you use negative words, they will stand out and get maximum attention.

In practice, this means avoiding negative words such as “can’t,” “don’t,” “won’t,” “couldn’t,” and “shouldn’t” and finding alternative ways to convey the same ideas using positive words.

Instead of “We can’t do that”, try “What if we tried this?” Instead of “I don’t think that’s a good idea”, you might say, “Let’s keep iterating to see if we can find an even better approach”. The idea is not to be passive-aggressive or evasive, but to be more thoughtful when dismissing ideas, suggesting alternatives, or even delivering bad news.

This gives more weight to any negative message that you need to deliver because you’re only using negative language when you must communicate that something is dire or needs a high level of attention.

It’s a challenge, but this is a muscle that you can exercise and strengthen over time.
